html:
Jean-Joseph Rabearivelo was a poet from Madagascar who wrote in French and Malagasy. He is often called the first modern African poet writing in French, and the greatest writer of Madagascar.

He grew up poor in Antananarivo in the first generation under French colonial rule, and left school early. He taught himself by reading French poetry and worked as a proofreader at a printing house. He also loved hainteny, the old Malagasy oral poems built on riddles and images.

His best-known books, Presque-Songes (Almost Dreams, 1934) and Traduit de la nuit (Translated from the Night, 1935), mix French verse with the dream-like images of Malagasy tradition. He published in both languages and wrote plays, stories and essays.

He felt shut out of both worlds: the colonial elite would not accept him as French, and he grew apart from his own society. When the authorities would not let him go to the Paris exhibition of 1937, he took his own life with cyanide, at about 36. Senghor put his poems in his famous 1948 anthology of Négritude poetry.
